query: For high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles intended for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, corrosion-related uses, and other applications requiring thermal stability, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their premelting and melting behavior and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing factor, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic fcc high-entropy-alloy (HEA) nanoparticles 2–20 nm in diameter, the temperatures for both premelting (surface softening) and complete melting are governed primarily by the magnitude of the *near-surface configurational entropy* (S_conf,surf). A larger S_conf,surf – produced by a chemically homogeneous, non-segregated surface – lowers the surface free energy and raises surface-diffusion barriers, thereby delaying the nucleation of a liquid layer and shifting premelting and melting to higher temperatures relative to particles with identical bulk composition but reduced S_conf,surf.
generation.material_initial_state: 5 ± 1 nm CoCrFeNiCu HEA nanoparticles prepared in two ways: (i) rapid co-reduction to yield a chemically homogeneous solid solution (high S_conf,surf); (ii) sequential reduction that drives Cu surface segregation, producing a core–shell arrangement and lower S_conf,surf. Crystal structure, size distribution, and overall composition are otherwise identical.
generation.intervention: In-situ heating of the two nanoparticle types in a transmission electron microscope (TEM) fitted with a nano-calorimetric holder, under identical vacuum/inert conditions.
generation.conditions: Linear heating ramp of 10 K min⁻¹ from 300 K to 1300 K at ≤10⁻⁷ Torr to suppress oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Near-surface configurational entropy (chemical disorder) which modulates surface free energy and atomic mobility.
generation.mechanism: Higher S_conf,surf creates a broad distribution of local bond strengths and strain fields that frustrate collective atomic rearrangements at the surface. This raises the activation energy for surface diffusion and reduces the driving force for surface melting, postponing the onset of a quasi-liquid layer and, consequently, the complete melting transition.
generation.predicted_outcome: Homogeneous high-S_conf,surf HEA nanoparticles will (1) exhibit the first signs of surface premelting (diffuse scattering, shape change) ~100 K above the temperature where these features appear in segregated (low-S_conf,surf) counterparts, and (2) reach complete melting ~150 K above the segregated particles and ~250 K above monometallic Ni nanoparticles of the same size measured in parallel.
generation.baseline: Monometallic Ni nanoparticles (5 ± 1 nm) heated under identical conditions provide a conventional size-dependent melting reference.
generation.boundary: Effect expected for single-phase fcc transition-metal HEA nanoparticles 2–20 nm in diameter where surface chemistry can be tuned without altering size, morphology, or crystallographic phase.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature offsets will depend on element choice and any inadvertent oxide formation; strain or electronic effects that accompany segregation could complicate interpretation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two CoCrFeNiCu nanoparticle batches as described. Verify surface compositions by atom-probe tomography and STEM-EDS line-scans to quantify S_conf,surf. Perform identical in-situ heating TEM experiments, recording diffraction patterns and high-resolution images throughout the ramp. Extract the temperatures at which (a) diffuse ring intensity rises (premelting) and (b) all Bragg reflections vanish (complete melting). Plot these temperatures against measured S_conf,surf.
measurements: Temperature of onset of diffuse scattering increase
Temperature at disappearance of Bragg spots (melting)
Surface diffusion coefficients from image analysis of edge atom mobility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if melting or premelting temperatures do *not* show a positive correlation with S_conf,surf—for example, if segregated, lower-entropy particles melt at the same or higher temperatures than homogeneous, high-entropy ones within experimental uncertainty (±20 K).
